newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Weak German tax take may lead to cut in estimates.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Weak German tax take may lead to cut in estimates.

text.p: Weak tax revenues during the first quarter may force Germany to revise up its forecast for revenue shortfalls this year, government sources said on Tuesday.

But the sources played down horror scenarios painted by the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), who have said that sluggish tax income and extra costs arising from high unemployment would blow away Bonn's bid to join Europe's single currency.

Tax revenues are being closely watched since they form one half of the equation in Bonn's bid this year to meet borrowing targets set by the Maastricht treaty and lead European monetary union (EMU) from the outset in 1999.
The most important target, and the one many countries are having the most difficulty meeting, is the restriction of budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product.
The sources said that total tax revenues during the first quarter of this year fell by 4.3 percent, compared to a year earlier, to 170.8 billion marks ($98.7 billion).
That opened the prospect that half-yearly tax projections due next month would have to be revised down from the forecast made last November.

The sources said especially weak revenues from assessed taxes pointed to "limited extra tax shortfalls" this year -- but the undershoot would not be as big as the 20 billion marks predicted by the SPD.

Those extra shortfalls would come on top of a cut in the government's view on tax revenues of eight billion marks made in its annual economic report in January. Then, revisions were made because final 1996 revenues came in five billion marks below target and the forecast of nominal economic growth in 1997 was lowered to 3.5 percent from 3.8 percent.

The SPD has also predicted that government spending would be inflated by 10 billion marks to support high German unemployment -- which last month stood at 4.5 million -- taking the budget deficit up to 3.4 percent of GDP.
But Finance Minister Theo Waigel said in a speech he was due to give in New York on Tuesday that he was optimistic of achieving the Maastricht treaty budget target.

"We are moving in the right direction regarding budget policies," Waigel said according to the text of his speech. "I am confident that we will force our total public deficit this year down to three percent of gross domestic product."

Waigel also said the government's forecast of 2.5 percent economic growth this year was realistic. Independent research groups, like Germany's authoritative six economic institutes, have forecast slower growth.
The sources said federal tax income in the first quarter was down 10.7 percent to 68.2 billion marks, while transfers to the European Union had jumped 28.9 percent to 14.3 billion.
Tax revenues in Germany's 16 federal states were down 2.5 percent to 78.9 billion marks and at municipal governments down 6.5 percent to 9.5 billion marks. ($ = 1.730 German Marks)
